name: Penile fracture
aliases: traumatic rupture of the corpus cavernosum

clinicalPearls: Rupture of the tunica albuginea of an erect corpus cavernosum, usually during vigorous intercourse or forced bending of the erect penis
The patient classically reports a sudden audible crack or pop, immediate pain, rapid detumescence, and swelling
The typical aubergine (eggplant) deformity results from a haematoma confined by Buck's fascia, giving a swollen, bruised, and often deviated penis
It is a surgical emergency, as prompt exploration and repair of the tunical defect give the best functional outcomes and reduce long-term erectile and deformity complications
Always assess for an associated urethral injury - blood at the meatus, frank haematuria, or difficulty voiding raises this concern
Diagnosis is largely clinical; ultrasound or MRI can localise the tear when the picture is equivocal, and retrograde urethrography or flexible cystoscopy evaluates the urethra
Delayed or conservative treatment carries higher rates of penile curvature, painful nodules, and erectile dysfunction than early surgical repair
reference.pathophysiology: During erection the tunica albuginea covering the corpora cavernosa is stretched thin and taut. An abrupt bending force against the rigid erect penis, most often when it slips out and strikes the perineum or pubis during intercourse, sharply raises intracavernosal pressure and tears the tunica. Blood escapes from the corpus cavernosum and, while contained by Buck's fascia, collects as a localised haematoma that produces the characteristic eggplant deformity; if Buck's fascia is also breached, bruising spreads more widely. Because the urethra and corpus spongiosum lie ventrally, a forceful injury can extend to cause a concurrent urethral rupture, which must be actively sought.
additionalDifferentials: Rupture of a superficial or dorsal penile vein or artery ('false fracture')
Penile haematoma without a tunical tear
Painful Peyronie's plaque or acute Peyronie's disease
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment for the eggplant deformity and a palpable tunical defect
Penile ultrasound to localise the tear
MRI of the penis when the diagnosis is uncertain
Retrograde urethrography to assess the urethra
Flexible cystoscopy where urethral injury is suspected
redFlags: Blood at the urethral meatus or gross haematuria, indicating urethral injury
Inability to pass urine or acute urinary retention
An expanding haematoma or bruising extending beyond Buck's fascia
reference.prognosis: Early surgical repair generally restores good erectile function with low rates of curvature and nodules; delay or non-operative management is associated with higher rates of penile deformity and erectile dysfunction.
pitfalls: Managing conservatively when early surgical exploration would give better functional results
Failing to evaluate the urethra and missing an associated urethral injury
Mistaking a ruptured superficial vessel ('false fracture') for a true tunical tear, or vice versa
Delaying theatre and increasing the risk of long-term penile deformity
management: Undertake prompt surgical exploration and repair of the tunica albuginea defect as the treatment of choice
Evacuate the haematoma and close the tear to restore anatomy and reduce long-term curvature
Actively assess for and repair any associated urethral injury identified on retrograde urethrography or cystoscopy
Provide analgesia and advise abstinence from sexual activity during healing
Arrange postoperative erectile-function follow-up and manage penile curvature or nodules if they develop
Refer urgently to urology given the time-critical nature of repair
